articles.title: Ian McKellen Honors His Friend Patrick Stewart: ‘The Most Respected and Beloved Actor of His Generation’
articles.summary: The two English actors first met with the Royal Shakespeare Company and starred together in the "X-Men" series.
articles.content: Ian McKellen has shared a tribute to his “ X-Men ” series co-star and longtime friend Patrick Stewart , who died Wednesday at the age of 86. McKellen and Stewart’s relationship goes back decades to their time as young theater actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company. They became inseparably tied together for general audiences when they starred opposite one another in Marvel’s “X-Men” film series, playing the frenemies Magneto and Professor X. Over the years, the two have shared a public friendship, often appearing at premieres for each other’s work and serving as two of British theater’s leading global ambassadors. In 2009, they starred in a West End production of “Waiting for Godot.” Related Stories Patrick Stewart Never Took His Gravitas for Granted, Even When He Was Subverting It Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Legend and Beloved Shakespearean Actor, Dead at 86 “Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues,” McKellen wrote in a statement posted to social media. “He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.” McKellen went on to recall Stewart’s decision to play Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” in the late ’80s — a role that solidified his presence in Hollywood and made him a household name for general audiences. “We first met as ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago but we weren’t in the same productions. articles.title: Matthew Weiner Exits Peacock, 101 Studios Series ‘The Chairman’ Starring Eddie Murphy (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.content: Matthew Weiner is no longer involved with the drama series “The Chairman” that is currently in development at Peacock , Variety has learned exclusively from sources. The project was first reported to be in the works at the streamer less than a month ago, with Eddie Murphy attached to star. According to sources, creative differences between Weiner and the show’s producers caused them to part ways. Related Stories Hugh Jackman Mourns 'X-Men' Co-Star Patrick Stewart: 'A Tremendous Friend and Man. I Learned So Much From Him' Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek's' Captain Picard and 'X-Men's' Charles Xavier, Dies at 86 A new showrunning team is already said to be in place and will be announced in the coming days. The show’s writers’ room has been placed on a two-week hiatus as the new creative leads come onboard. Exact plot details for “The Chairman” remain under wraps. Should it get picked up to series, it would be the first live-action series in which Murphy has starred since his days as a cast member on “Saturday Night Live.” The series will be produced by Universal Television and 101 Studios , which is run by “Yellowstone” executive producer David Glasser. 101 is currently under a first-look film and television deal at NBCUniversal that began in January. “The Chairman” will also be the first project to come out of ex-Paramount boss Chris McCarthy’s deal at NBCUniversal, which was first reported in November 2025 and put him in a consulting role on the studio’s relationship with Glasser and 101. Murphy serves as a producer “The Chairman” in addition to starring. Weiner is best known for creating the seminal TV drama “Mad Men,” which aired for seven seasons on AMC and won 16 Emmy Awards. “The Chairman,” assuming it is to be greenlit, would have marked Weiner’s first TV writing credit since 2018, when he created the Amazon Prime Video series “The Romanoffs.”

articles.title: Patrick Stewart Never Took His Gravitas for Granted, Even When He Was Subverting It
articles.summary: The English actor, who died Thursday, could take command of a scene with a single syllable. But he didn't stop there, rewarding audiences who followed him everywhere.
articles.content: No one is ever upset, or even disappointed, when Sir Patrick Stewart pops up onscreen. Whether he’s the umpteenth cameo in a Marvel movie or a surprise addition to a sprawling Super Bowl commercial , the master of Shakespeare and generational captain is always greeted by audiences with eager anticipation, if not outright glee. But Stewart, who died Thursday afternoon from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, didn’t treat his warm regard as a given. He saw the respect he earned throughout his towering career as an opportunity for what to do next — not for easy paychecks from familiar parts, but to push himself into new territory and delight audiences all over again. Seth MacFarlane (who worked with Stewart on “Family Guy,” “American Dad,” and “Ted”) was producing, and Stewart was starring as a past-his-prime British news anchor attempting to start anew in America. The premium cable network gave the comedy, from “Bored to Death” creator Jonathan Ames, a straight-to-series order with a two-season commitment. And that’s exactly how long it lasted: two, 10-episode seasons, neither of which earned the acclaim or viewership the network expected. Stewart snagged a Golden Globe nomination (his last of three total, following nods for the 2005 TV remake of “The Lion in the Winter” and 1999’s two-episode “Moby Dick” adaptation), but reviews were middling and interest fell off quickly. I’ll admit: I don’t remember much of the show’s plot, in part because it wasn’t as “grand” as I initially thought . articles.title: William Shatner and ‘Star Trek’ Family Mourn Patrick Stewart With Picard Tributes: ‘Godspeed, Captain’
articles.content: Tributes from across the “ Star Trek ” franchise are pouring in for Patrick Stewart following the news of his death at 86. articles.title: Bleecker Street CEO on Why the Social Media Suppression of ‘Musk’ Is About Much More Than Film
articles.summary: The nearly 4-hour documentary about Elon Musk struggled at the box office but has had a surge of interest in PVOD pre-sales.
articles.content: Elon Musk has given $276 million to Republican groups and his super PAC since this July ahead of the midterm elections, the New York Times recently reported . But “ Musk ,” Alex Gibney ‘s documentary about the world’s first trillionaire, is not a political film . Or at least not for the majority of its nearly 4-hour runtime. It’s a film about this singular man’s influence on the world and covers far more ground than his involvement with Trump administration or the midterms. But the documentary has been treated as political by every social media platform the film has tried to advertise on. Meta and YouTube each pulled distributor Bleecker Street ‘s paid trailer for the film before later restoring it , saying its removal was in error. TikTok on the weekend “Musk” expanded to 500 theaters “permanently” suspended the film’s account because it said it repeatedly violated its policies of paying to boost what it viewed as political content, and it only reinstated the account after two days, an eternity if you’re chasing weekend box office. X, which is owned by Musk, predictably didn’t play ball at all. Related Stories Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Legend and Beloved Shakespearean Actor, Dead at 86 Curry Barker Drops Surprise New Short Film ‘Mama Bear’ — Watch Gibney has not been shy highlighting the “accidental” bans that ads for his film have had to endure. His distributor Bleecker Street behind the scenes has been fighting these battles. The film’s box office, just $672K in three weeks, has been extremely disappointing. In response, Bleecker is moving up the PVOD release date of “Musk” to November 6 after slating it for late in November. And the response has been enormous. articles.title: The Netflix Original Movie Experiment Has Failed — and Netflix Will Be All the Better for It
articles.summary: Netflix spent the last 10 years trying to render movie theaters obsolete. Now the company is giving up just in time to avoid becoming obsolete itself.
articles.content: In April 2025, somehow only 18 months ago, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos participated in a public conversation that began with Time magazine’s editor-in-chief asking him a simple question: “Have you destroyed Hollywood?” It was meant as a cheeky icebreaker, and Sarandos — a smirk cracking across his face — gave the exact response you would expect from a disruptor of his wealth and power: “No, we’re saving Hollywood.” They were saving Hollywood from the very reason it exists in the first place, and the reason — the only reason — why it continues to exert a peerlessly disproportionate influence on the collective imagination: movie theaters. “We’re in a period of transition,” Sarandos elaborated later in the panel. “Folks grew up thinking, ‘I want to make movies on a gigantic screen and have strangers watch them [and to have them] play in the theater for two months and people cry and sold-out shows’ …It’s an outdated concept.” Related Stories Rare Stanley Kubrick Interview Headed to TCM’s ‘Plot Thickens’ Podcast as Bonus Episode AMC Releases ‘Dune 3’ Two-Headed Sandworm Popcorn Bucket That Manages to Look Even More NSFW Cut to: October 2026. Hollywood is in a more precarious state than ever, and Netflix just rented out New York’s biggest AMC to stage a trailer premiere for the most crucial movie the company has ever made, an event where “Narnia” director Greta Gerwig was interviewed by Stephen Colbert in front of a massive IMAX screen as an audience of journalists munched on candy and popcorn. The screen was gigantic. Gerwig cried. When “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” opens in theaters next February, it will play there exclusively for (almost) two months before it’s available to watch on Netflix. Sarandos was right about one thing: We are in a period of transition. It’s just not the transition he had in mind. articles.title: ‘Wicker’ Is Even Better — and Hornier — in 4DX
articles.summary: Last night, audiences got to experience an event that intensified the pleasures of the year's most surprisingly romantic film in extremely visceral ways.
articles.content: Ever since 4DX technology debuted in 2009 for Seoul screenings of James Cameron’s “Avatar,” the immersive format has been associated primarily with spectacles and franchise films; if you’ve been to a 4DX auditorium, you probably went to see a Marvel movie or a “ Fast and Furious ” sequel. The idea seems to be that 4DX — a presentation system that “enhances” movies with physical effects like shaking seats, wind, flashing lights, snow, water, and scents — is best utilized in action films where the onscreen chaos is intensified by the chaos of being yanked around in your chair while nozzles spray air and water in your face. For years, I avoided 4DX like the plague after an ill-advised trip to see “Maleficent: Mistress of Evil.” When motion sickness set in before the end of the first reel, I figured I had experienced enough 4DX to last me for the rest of my life. Then last year, while writing a piece comparing six release formats for “ One Battle After Another ,” I gave 4DX another shot and was surprised by how much I enjoyed it. Seeing Paul Thomas Anderson’s masterpiece with effects that included air blasting in my ear to simulate gunshots and the seat rocking to simulate Sean Penn’s masturbation added an unexpected dimension to the viewing experience. Related Stories Yes, That’s a Wicker Penis: Inside Alexander Skarsgård’s Wild ‘Wicker’ Transformation Will ‘Wicker’ Be Black Bear’s First Big Breakout? Since then, I’ve caught a couple more movies in 4DX, from an epic that typically uses the format (“The Odyssey”) to a contained thriller that barely uses it at all (“Verity”). Then, last night, I caught the “Citizen Kane” of 4DX movies, the one that uses the format the way it should have always been implemented — not as a form of cinematic shock treatment designed to amplify onscreen violence, but as an expression of sensual pleasure. articles.title: death at age 86
articles.content: Sir Patrick Stewart , the star of Star Trek: The Next Generation , Star Trek: Picard , the X-Men film franchise and many other movies, TV shows and stage plays, died October 28 at his home in Los Angeles following a battle with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. He was 86. “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” the statement reads. “He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.” Stewart, the distinguished stage and screen actor and New York Times best-selling author whose career spanned nearly six decades, was a three-time Olivier Award winner and a Tony Award nominee for his stage work, including numerous Shakespeare productions. He won a Grammy in 1995 and received multiple Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations for his work across television and film. In the 2001 New Year Honours list, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Stewart an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE), and in 2010, she knighted him for services to drama. He was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1996. Born July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, West Riding of Yorkshire, England, Stewart left school at 15 to perform in local theater and made his professional stage debut in 1959 at the Theatre Royal, Bristol in a production of Cyrano de Bergerac . Stewart became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and in 1967 made his debut TV appearance on Coronation Street . He made his Broadway debut in 1970 as Snout in Peter Brook’s 1970 production A Midsummer Night’s Dream. RELATED: James McAvoy Pi

articles.content: Should Monarch: Legacy of Monsters return for a third season on Apple TV , it will likely look somewhat different — both in front of and behind the camera. articles.summary: He also worked on ‘Bewitched,’ ‘Get Smart,’ ‘The Andy Griffith Show,’ ‘The Governor & J.J.’ and ‘See No Evil, Hear No Evil’ and came up with the villain King Tut for ‘Batman.’
articles.content: Earl Barret, the veteran comedy writer who co-developed the Ted Knight-starring Too Close for Comfort and worked on more than 30 other series, including Bewitched , Get Smart , Batman and The Andy Griffith Show , has died. He was 94. Barret died Oct. 22 of natural causes at his home in Sherman Oaks, his daughter, J.K. Barret, announced. He was a “lifelong learner with a keen, curious mind and a gift for impeccable comic timing,” she said. The Ohio native also wrote for My Favorite Martian , My Three Sons , My Mother the Car , I Spy , The Wild Wild West , Julia , The Bob Newhart Show , Sanford and Son and Welcome Back, Kotter . The American adaptation, which ran for six seasons (1980-87) on ABC and in syndication, revolved around Knight’s Henry Rush, a cartoonist who works out of the San Francisco home he shares with his wife (Nancy Dussault) and adult daughters (Deborah Van Valkenburgh, Lydia Cornell). Barret and Sultan first worked together on the 1969-70 CBS comedy The Governor & J.J. , starring Dan Dailey and Julie Sommars. They continued with NBC’s The Partners (Don Adams’ first series after Get Smart ), CBS’ The Sandy Duncan Show , ABC’s Holmes and Yoyo and The New Odd Couple and the CTV’s Check It Out (Adams starred on that one, too). The pair also were among the credited writers on the 1989 feature See No Evil, Hear No Evil , directed by Arthur Hiller and starring Richard Pryor and Gene Wilder . articles.title: TV Ratings: Why Fox News Suffered Its Largest Pre-Election Month Drop in the Past Decade
articles.summary: It still leads rivals MS NOW and CNN by wide margins, however.
articles.content: In the “two things can be true” category: Fox News still holds sizable ratings leads in cable news over CNN and MS NOW . It also suffered the largest year-to-year ratings drop in the month before an election in the past 10 years. Nielsen ratings for October show Fox News averaging 1.68 million viewers in primetime and 1.01 million for the full day. Both are comfortably ahead of MS NOW (925,000 primetime, 588,000 full day) and CNN (598,000, 402,000). In the key news demographic of adults 25-54, things are a bit closer, but Fox’s totals of 145,000 in primetime and 98,000 for the total day still lead. CNN had 107,000 in the demo in primetime and 60,000 for the full day, to 95,000 and 62,000 for MS NOW. Fox also had the five most watched cable news shows, led by The Five at 2.7 million daily viewers. Fox News is also touting its online strength, citing 3.8 billion YouTube views for 2026 so far (as measured by social media analytics firm Emplifi), compared with 2.96 billion for MS NOW and 2.36 billion for CNN. As for the second true thing: In the past decade, none of the three biggest cable news outlets has suffered a decline in the month before a national election as big as Fox News did this year. Compared to October 2025, Fox News slipped by 28 percent in primetime viewers and 27 percent for the full day. The network’s adults 25-54 audience fell by more than 30 percent. MS NOW and CNN both had double-digit percentage gains in primetime versus a year earlier; MS NOW also did so for the full day, while CNN had a more modest 3 percent bump. (It’s worth noting that the latter two were also at low points in 2025, and big percentage gains are more likely when the starting point is lower.) articles.content: Ernie Johnson, the long-serving host of Inside the NBA on TNT and ESPN , is stepping down. In an Instagram video Wednesday, Johnson said that this season — his 37th — will be his last as the host of the NBA highlights and analysis show. Johnson became host of Inside the NBA with its second season in 1990 and has been at the helm ever since, wrangling and playing off of analysts Kenny Smith (since 1998), Charles Barkley (since 2000) and Shaquille O’Neal (since 2011). “I’ve long described it as a ‘get to’ job — I’m still amazed I get to do this for a living,” Johnson said in the video (watch it in full below). “… This will be my last season. Now after 37 seasons, it’s time.” Barkley pre-empted Johnson’s announcement somewhat in September, saying that he planned to retire from Inside the NBA alongside Johnson after the 2026-27 season. “Right now, unless Ernie changes his mind, next year is my last year for 100%,” Barkley said on The Bill Simmons Podcast . The 70-year-old Johnson had heart bypass surgery in 2025, and while he said he feels “great” and isn’t under doctor’s orders to scale back, he wants to use more of his time to be with his family, including his five grandchildren. articles.content: Tom Cruise, Jack Nicholson and Demi Moore are replaced by Tom Blyth, Bradley Whitford and Krysta Rodriguez The new regime at Lincoln Center Theater has a novel pitch to theatergoers: Since you’ve already seen the movie, why not see the stage version? It started last season with “Ragtime,” and continues now with “A Few Good Men,” which opened Thursday at the Vivian Beaumont Theater. Coming soon at that revered venue is “The Sound of Music.” Before there was the 1992 movie starring Tom Cruise, Demi Moore and Jack Nicholson, Aaron Sorkin wrote the play “A Few Good Men,” which opened on Broadway in 1989. It didn’t exactly impress the people at the Tony Awards, since it received only one nomination, for lead actor Tom Hulce. It was quite a snub. When it came to Best Play nominations, Sorkin’s big message drama about corruption in the army lost out to the boulevard comedy “Lettice & Lovage,” a piece of fluff designed to showcase the star power of Maggie Smith. LTC’s revival of Sorkin’s court-martial drama makes it clear that the Tony Awards got it right. “A Few Good Men” is a creaky old play. Two Marines (Lavel Schley and Collin Kelly-Sordelet) are accused of murdering PFC William T. Santiago (Daniel Velez), at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. Were the two men acting alone, or had they been ordered by their superior LtCol Nathan R. Jessep (Bradley Whitford) to bind, shave and gag Santiago? Despite its military milieu, “A Few Good Men” begins much like a rom-com with an overly contrived fight between a man and woman who could not be more different. articles.content: Sir Patrick Stewart , the beloved stage and screen star known for his role as Jean-Luc Picard in “ Star Trek : The Next Generation,” has died at the age of 86 years old. News of his death was first reported by The New York Times . A fixture of the stage and screen for the past six decades, Stewart was equally active in the realms of classical drama and contemporary genre entertainment. Born in Mirfield, England in 1940, Stewart attended the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School and began acting with the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. He remained a member through 1982, playing many of the Bard’s most iconic roles and becoming a fixture of British television. It would have already been enough to call his acting career a successful one, but Hollywood stardom came calling for him in the late ’80s. He played the role for seven seasons of “The Next Generation” and went on to reprise it in four films. He notably reprised the role in the final years of his life in “Star Trek: Picard,” a three-season series that caught up with an older version of the character and allowed Stewart to deconstruct his most iconic role. Stewart’s most notable film role arguably came in the “ X-Men ” franchise, in which he played Professor Charles Xavier. He first took on the role of the mutant superhero team leader in Bryan Singer’s 2000 film “X-Men.” He would continue to play the character for the remainder of his life, appearing in seven films for 20th Century Fox and then bringing the character into the Marvel Cinematic Universe after Disney acquired the IP. articles.content: Anyone who saw Sandra Wollner’s perversely creepy previous film , “The Trouble with Being Born,” might be left having no idea what to expect from her follow-up. That film was built around a child-sized android cast in resemblance to her master’s missing daughter — and it’s more than implied he’s sexually assaulting the girl, too. Disturbing as it was, “The Trouble with Being Born” also announced Wollner’s aptitude for capturing grief from peculiar, underseen angles. And so her next movie, “ Everytime ,” while more generously empathetic, also takes on loss from a mind-bending perspective we’re not going to spoil. Since winning in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard, this German entry for the Best International Feature Film Oscar has bewitched festivalgoers from Toronto to New York. articles.summary: Before we crown the A24 hit a contender, let's do the numbers.
articles.content: Everybody’s talking about the A24 documentary “ You Can See Everything,” and many Oscar prognosticators are jumping on board the Best Picture bandwagon . Don’t buy the hype. While there’s a lot to admire about Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s entertaining nonfiction approach to parsing the distorted reality of disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes just before she went to prison, it’s still a long road for a surprise box-office documentary hit ($45 million domestic and counting) to garner enough Oscar votes for a Best Picture nomination. Related Stories Barbara Barrie, Oscar-Nominated ‘Breaking Away’ and ‘Private Benjamin’ Star, Dies at 95 A Flop at the Chinese Box Office Shows AI Still Has a Tough Road Ahead in Theaters The folks who believe it’s possible are listening to the current buzz and noise, much of it from younger movie fans on social media, and the film ‘s undeniable heat. A24’s brilliant “no spoilers” marketing campaign has pushed more moviegoers than usual into theaters early in the run. But the Academy membership is still senior-centric. Step One: Critic group wins. This week’s Gotham nomination for Best Documentary Feature is a start. The movie needs to land awards from the NYFCC, LAFCA, and NSFC. The Golden Globes will be no help, as they do not give a documentary prize. Critic support will add prestige and convince laggards to watch the movie on the Academy portal. Step Two: Lure international voters. “YCSE” is an American movie, even if it confronts alternate reality issues familiar to everyone. It has yet to open overseas. Recognition from the BAFTAs (it will be eligible) would show support outside North America.
